# ggpyramid

<!-- badges: start -->
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/matanhakim/ggpyramid/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/matanhakim/ggpyramid/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

ggpyramid is a [ggplot2](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org) extension for building
population pyramids: back-to-back bar charts of a population by age group and
sex. A pyramid is one more layer in an ordinary ggplot, so scales, facets,
themes and further layers work as they do anywhere else in ggplot2.

## Installation

Install the released version of ggpyramid from CRAN with:

``` r
install.packages("ggpyramid")
```

Or the development version from
[GitHub](https://github.com/matanhakim/ggpyramid) with:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("matanhakim/ggpyramid")
```

## Example

`geom_pyramid()` draws the bars and `coord_pyramid()` the axes. The bars sum a
value when one is mapped, as here, and count rows when it is not, so they
accept aggregated tables and individual records alike. `europe_pop` holds the
population of four European countries in 2004 and 2024, from Eurostat.

```{r pyramid, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 150}
library(ggplot2)
library(ggpyramid)

france <- subset(europe_pop, country == "France" & year == 2024)

ggplot(france, aes(x = population, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_pyramid(width = 1, colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  coord_pyramid(age_axis = "centre") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_pyramid()
```

`denominator` turns the bars into shares of the panel or of each side, and
each facet gets its own denominator. `geom_pyramid_outline()` draws a second
population as a stepped line over the bars:

```{r compare, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6, dpi = 150}
ggplot(europe_pop, aes(x = population, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_pyramid(data = ~ subset(.x, year == 2024), denominator = "total") +
  geom_pyramid_outline(data = ~ subset(.x, year == 2004), denominator = "total") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  coord_pyramid() +
  facet_wrap(vars(country)) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = "2024",
    caption = "Share of the population. The outline shows 2004."
  ) +
  theme_pyramid()
```

`geom_pyramid_text()` labels each bar at its end, on both sides:

```{r labels, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 150}
ireland <- subset(europe_pop, country == "Ireland" & year == 2024)

ggplot(ireland, aes(x = population, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_pyramid(denominator = "side") +
  geom_pyramid_text(
    denominator = "side",
    labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 0.1),
    size = 2.6
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_percent(),
    expand = expansion(mult = 0.15)
  ) +
  coord_pyramid(age_axis = "centre") +
  labs(x = "Share of each sex", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_pyramid()
```

`vignette("ggpyramid")` covers the rest: placing the age axis, subgroups
within each side, vertical pyramids, and how the two sides are drawn.

## Related work

[apyramid](https://cran.r-project.org/package=apyramid) builds a complete
pyramid from one function call. `geom_pyramid()` in
[ggstats](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ggstats) is a layer that mirrors
bars by their position in a stack. ggpyramid takes the side from a variable
and adds the coordinate system, labels and outlines that a pyramid needs, each
as a separate ggplot2 component.
